bib.title: ShareGPT4V: Improving Large Multi-Modal Models with Better Captions

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed for lineage only.

question: Does replacing short, low-quality image captions with long, detailed GPT4-Vision captions improve modality alignment in large multi-modal models, in both pre-training and supervised fine-tuning?
hypothesis: Existing low-quality captions impede vision-language alignment, so higher-quality, highly descriptive captions improve LMM performance at both stages.
contributions: We point out the fact that existing low-quality captions can impede the alignment between vision and language modalities of LMMs and we verify it with experimental results.
We introduce the ShareGPT4V dataset: 100K GPT4-Vision captions and 1.2M captions from a caption model trained on them.
We develop ShareGPT4V-7B, an LMM with a simple architecture that performs strongly across multi-modal benchmarks.

method.summary: About 100K images were captioned by GPT4-Vision using a base prompt plus a data-source-specific prompt. These were used to fine-tune a general caption model (Share-Captioner) that captioned 1.2M further images for pre-training. A LLaVA-1.5-style 7B model was then pre-trained on the 1.2M captions (vision encoder partly unfrozen) and SFT'd on the LLaVA-1.5 665K mix with its 23K detailed-description items replaced by 23K of the GPT4-Vision captions.

prompts.text: You are a powerful image captioner.

Instead of describing the imaginary content, only describing the content one can determine confidently from the image. Do not describe the contents by itemizing them in list form. Minimize aesthetic descriptions as much as possible.

Create detailed captions describing the contents of the given image. Include the object types and colors, counting the objects, object actions, precise object locations, texts, double-checking relative positions between objects, etc.

Create a detailed caption describing the contents of the given image. This image is about actor/actress <actor_name> or maybe his/her character. Include the colors, person actions, expressions, precise person and object locations, person/character names, etc.

Create detailed captions describing the contents of the given worldwide landmark image. There is some information that may be used to identify the landmark: <landmark>. Include the objects, colors, perspectives, etc.
Create detailed captions describing the contents of the given art image. Include the objects, colors, art style, art genre, etc.
Create detailed captions describing the contents of the given image. Pay more attention to the text contents and the information they convey.

limits: All evidence is on a 7B (and 13B baseline) LLaVA-1.5 recipe; larger scales and other architectures are not tested beyond the SFT swap on three models.
The authors concede they focus on the lightweight 7B scale and state the goal is not a new SOTA architecture.

Captions come from a proprietary teacher (GPT4-Vision); the 1.2M set inherits its errors and the paper reports no hallucination rate or factuality audit of the captions, only a 100-sample human preference test with 10 volunteers.
Single runs, no seeds or variance; gains of about 1 point on some benchmarks cannot be separated from noise. Some competitor numbers were re-implemented (starred).
Pre-training objective, optimizer, schedule, warmup, precision, hardware for training, and Share-Captioner fine-tuning details are not stated.
Paper's own SFT experiment replaces detailed-description data with captions, mixing a quality change with a distribution change (sources are broader than COCO).
Fig 11 dialog example shows the model confidently misidentifying two characters as Steve Jobs and Isaac Newton, which the paper does not discuss.
